canonical_statement: The study assessed bleeding frequency and first APTT in relation to BMI among patients receiving uncapped weight-based IV UFH for medical cardiac indications.
This was a retrospective cohort analysis at Saint Marys Hospital, a 1157-bed tertiary academic medical center in Rochester, Minnesota.
The source reports enrollment from February 1, 2002 through November 31, 2003; the reported end date is not a valid calendar date and is preserved without correction.
Eligible patients were age 15 years or older, had a medical cardiac indication, and were prescribed the computerized weight-based UFH nomogram.
Patients receiving UFH for less than 6 hours without a 6-hour APTT were excluded.
Patients without research authorization or with a documented UFH allergy, including heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, were excluded.
Patients concomitantly receiving a fibrinolytic, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor, or another antithrombotic agent other than warfarin were excluded.
The UFH regimen used an initial 60 U/kg IV bolus followed by a 12 U/kg/h continuous IV infusion calculated from actual body weight without initial dose caps.

canonical_statement: The primary analyses used Mantel-Haenszel chi-square tests, Kruskal-Wallis and pairwise Wilcoxon tests, t tests, and multivariable logistic regression with prespecified candidate covariates.
No power analysis was performed; the study used a convenience sample of consecutive patients treated with the computerized UFH nomogram.
The institutional review board approved the study and waived informed consent.
Of 2411 patients meeting initial inclusion criteria, 1357 were excluded and 1054 were included in the analysis.

canonical_statement: The retrospective design limits causal inference.
The study did not directly compare uncapped UFH initiation with a regimen using capped initial bolus and infusion limits.
The study did not assess efficacy outcomes such as additional thromboembolic events and was underpowered for these infrequent outcomes.
The investigators could not determine whether some patients had UFH exposure in the emergency department or another institution before nomogram initiation.
Concomitant aspirin, clopidogrel, and warfarin could have affected bleeding, and the available data could not establish that use of these agents was similar across BMI quartiles.
The authors concluded that obese patients did not have increased bleeding risk when treated with actual-body-weight UFH without capped initial dosing.
